column2: On the authority of Abū Ruqayyah Tamīm ibn Aws al-Dārī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said: “The religion is sincere counsel (naṣīḥah).” We said: “To whom?”
He said: “To Allah, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims and to their common people.” Reported by Muslim.

His words, “The religion is sincere counsel”: this is a comprehensive statement showing the importance of sincere counsel in the religion, and that it is its foundation and mainstay. Included under it is what came in the hadith of Jibrīl, in which the Messenger ﷺ explained Islam, faith and excellence,
and called that “religion”, saying: “This was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” Similar to this sentence is his ﷺ saying, “Ḥajj is ʿArafah”,
because it is the greatest pillar of Ḥajj, without which the Ḥajj is lost.
It has come in the Mustakhraj of Abū ʿAwānah that the Prophet ﷺ repeated this sentence, “The religion is sincere counsel”, three times;
in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim it is without repetition. When the Companions heard this concern and emphasis on sincere counsel, and that it held this great rank, they said: To whom, O Messenger of Allah?

He answered them with the five mentioned in the hadith. A number of scholars have explained these five, and among the best of that is what has come from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Ṣalāḥ in his book Ṣiyānat Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim min al-Ikhlāl wa-l-Ghalaṭ

wa-Ḥimāyatuhu min al-Isqāṭ wa-l-Saqaṭ, where he said (pp. 223–224): “Naṣīḥah is a comprehensive word that means the counsellor's undertaking all kinds of good for the one counselled, in intention and in action. Sincere counsel to Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, is:

affirming His oneness, describing Him with all the attributes of perfection and majesty, declaring Him free of whatever opposes and contradicts them, avoiding disobedience to Him, carrying out acts of obedience to Him and what He loves with sincerity, loving for His sake and hating for His sake, striving against whoever disbelieves in Him, the Exalted, and the like,

and calling to that and urging it. Sincere counsel to His Book is: believing in it, revering it and declaring it free [of imperfection], reciting it as it deserves to be recited, abiding by its commands and prohibitions, understanding its sciences and parables, pondering its verses, calling to it, and defending it against the distortions of the extremists and the attacks of the heretics.

Sincere counsel to His Messenger ﷺ is close to that: believing in him and in what he brought, honouring and revering him, holding fast to obedience to him, reviving his Sunnah, drawing out (istishārah—so in the text; in what Ibn Rajab quotes from him: istithārah) its sciences and spreading them,

being hostile to whoever is hostile to him and to it and loyal to whoever is loyal to him and to it, taking on his character, adopting his manners, loving his family and Companions, and the like. Sincere counsel to the leaders of the Muslims, meaning their caliphs and rulers, is: helping them in the truth and obeying them in it,

alerting and reminding them gently and kindly, refraining from rebelling against them, supplicating for their success, and urging others to do the same. Sincere counsel to the common people of the Muslims, who here are those other than the ones in authority among them, is: guiding them to what is good for them,

teaching them the matters of their religion and their worldly life, concealing their faults, meeting their needs, supporting them against their enemies, defending them, avoiding cheating and envying them, loving for them what one loves for oneself and disliking for them what one dislikes for oneself, and the like.”
An explanation of the great importance of sincere counsel and its lofty place in the religion.
An explanation of to whom sincere counsel is owed.
Encouragement to give sincere counsel in the five [areas] mentioned in the hadith.
The Companions' eagerness to learn the matters of the religion, shown by their asking to whom sincere counsel is owed.
The word “religion” is applied to deeds,
since he called sincere counsel “religion”.
